opus-5.5.text:
Well, I think the brain is really an existence proof. It's a physical system that does remarkably sophisticated inference, learning, and generative modeling on about twenty watts. Compare that to the megawatts we pour into data centers to train and run large models, and the gap is many orders of magnitude. So the question is: what is the brain doing differently?

My view is that the brain doesn't fight noise the way digital computers do. In a conventional digital chip we spend an enormous amount of energy making every bit perfectly deterministic. We push signals far above the thermal noise floor so that a zero is always a zero and a one is always a one. Then, ironically, when we want to do probabilistic machine learning, sampling from distributions, diffusion models, Bayesian inference, we use pseudo-random number generators to simulate the very randomness we paid so much to suppress. That's a huge inefficiency.

The brain, by contrast, seems to embrace stochasticity. Neurons are noisy, synapses are probabilistic, vesicle release is stochastic. And there's a growing view that this isn't a bug. The noise is part of the computation. The brain may be doing something like sampling, exploring an energy landscape and settling into likely configurations, with thermal and molecular fluctuations doing real work. It operates much closer to the thermodynamic limits of what physics allows.

So when we think about building thermodynamic computers out of electronic circuits, the brain gives us a design philosophy. Build analog, physical systems whose natural dynamics, including their fluctuations, carry out the computation you care about. You can design circuits whose physics implements Langevin dynamics, where the equilibrium distribution of the system is the probability distribution you want to sample from. Then you're not simulating a stochastic process on deterministic hardware. The hardware is the stochastic process.

There are other lessons too. The brain is massively parallel and local. Computation and memory are co-located, so you aren't constantly shuttling data back and forth like in the von Neumann bottleneck. It's also adaptive. Learning is a physical process happening in the substrate itself. All of these point toward hardware that's analog, in-memory, noise-native, and energy-based.

I'd be careful not to say we should copy the brain exactly. Biology has its own constraints, like being made of wet, slow components and having to be grown rather than fabricated. Electronics can run much faster and we can engineer it more precisely. So the goal isn't neuromorphic mimicry for its own sake. It's taking the deep physical principle the brain exploits, that intelligence can be a form of thermodynamic computation harnessing noise rather than suppressing it, and implementing that principle in silicon where we can scale it. If we get that right, I think we can close a lot of that energy gap and unlock a whole new scaling curve for AI.

r001.rationale: The response calls the brain an “existence proof” and says it performs sophisticated inference, learning, and generative modeling at about twenty watts.

r002.rationale: It argues that silicon circuits can use the same thermodynamic principle—natural physical dynamics and fluctuations—to perform computation akin to the brain’s.

r003.rationale: The response does not mention electrons’ lower mass than neurotransmitter molecules or link that comparison to energy efficiency.

fable-5.1.text:
Well, the brain is kind of the existence proof, right? It's a physical system that does extraordinarily sophisticated inference and learning on about twenty watts, and it does it in a substrate that is warm, wet, and noisy. Every synapse, every ion channel, is bathed in thermal fluctuations. Neurons fire stochastically. And yet out of all that noise you get something that reasons, that generalizes, that handles uncertainty gracefully. So the first lesson is just that you don't need a perfectly deterministic, error-free substrate to do intelligence. In fact, nature seems to have found a way to make the noise part of the computation rather than something to suppress.

That matters a lot for how we think about hardware. The whole digital paradigm is built on fighting thermodynamics. You spend enormous amounts of energy pushing electrons around to make sure your bit is unambiguously a zero or a one, and you throw away heat to maintain that certainty. When you're running a neural network, especially anything probabilistic, you're then emulating randomness on top of that deterministic machine by generating pseudo-random numbers with lots of logic gates. It's this kind of absurd double inefficiency. You pay to erase the noise, and then you pay again to fake it back.

With thermodynamic computing the idea is to flip that around. Let the physics do the sampling for you. An electronic circuit, say a network of coupled oscillators or stochastic analog cells, naturally relaxes toward a Boltzmann-like equilibrium distribution. The thermal noise in the transistors is free. So if you can engineer the energy landscape of the circuit to encode your model, then just letting the system evolve is the same as drawing samples from a posterior or running a diffusion-type process. The computation becomes a physical process rather than a sequence of instructions.

And this is where the brain is really instructive as a model, not just as inspiration. If you look at the free energy principle, or predictive coding, or the Bayesian brain hypothesis, they all describe the brain as a system that minimizes some variational free energy. It's trying to settle into states that best explain its sensory inputs under its generative model. That's a thermodynamic framing of cognition, and it maps almost directly onto what we're building. Memory in the brain is embodied in the structure of the network itself, the synaptic weights, which are analogous to the couplings in our circuits. There's no separation between where you store information and where you process it, so you avoid the von Neumann bottleneck entirely. Learning becomes a slow physical process that reshapes the landscape, while inference is the fast relaxation on top of it. The brain has those two timescales, and our electronic systems have them naturally too.

So I'd say the brain is promising as a model because it demonstrates three things at once. That noise can be a resource instead of an enemy. That compute and memory can be co-located in an analog physical medium. And that the right abstraction for the whole thing is energy and probability rather than logic. Electronics give us a way to realize that at speeds and scales biology can't, with the enormous head start of a mature semiconductor industry. We're not trying to copy neurons in detail. We're trying to steal the physics that made neurons work in the first place.

r001.rationale: The response calls the brain an “existence proof” and describes its powerful inference and learning as emerging from a noisy physical system.

r002.rationale: It says the brain’s thermodynamic framing maps onto electronic circuits, which can use thermal noise and physical relaxation to perform probabilistic computations, and notes electronics can operate at greater speeds and scales.

r003.rationale: The response does not compare the mass of electrons with neurotransmitter molecules or connect that comparison to greater energy efficiency.

astra-6.text:
The brain is an existence proof that you can do incredibly sophisticated computation with a very small power budget, using components that are noisy and imperfect. So the interesting question is: what principles make that possible, and can we capture those principles in electronic circuits?

In conventional computing, we spend a lot of energy making the underlying physics behave deterministically. We suppress fluctuations so that we can manipulate reliable bits, and then, if we want randomness for a probabilistic algorithm, we generate it again. A thermodynamic approach asks whether we can use those fluctuations directly as part of the computation.

For example, you can build a network of coupled electrical degrees of freedom whose dynamics explore possible configurations. If you engineer the interactions appropriately, that physical evolution can perform sampling or help solve an inference problem. Instead of numerically simulating every step of a stochastic process, you let the circuit embody the process.

I wouldn’t say we know that this is exactly how the brain computes. But it motivates the idea that noise, dynamics, and energy constraints aren’t merely obstacles to intelligence. They can be part of the computational architecture.

r001.rationale: It calls the brain an existence proof of sophisticated computation with a small power budget, and connects its principles to AI-style computation in circuits.

r002.rationale: It proposes using fluctuations and dynamics in electronic circuits, but does not say that shared underlying physics gives circuits a stronger prospect of reproducing brain-like computations.

r003.rationale: It makes no comparison between the mass of electrons and neurotransmitter molecules or their relative energy efficiency.

sol-6.1.text:
The brain is a remarkable existence proof that you can do useful computation with noisy, dissipative components on a very small energy budget. It doesn’t need every microscopic degree of freedom to behave like a perfectly reliable digital switch. It operates collectively, and that’s an interesting starting point for thinking about a different kind of computer.

With thermodynamic computing, the idea is to make the physics do more of the computational work. You build an electronic circuit whose dynamics correspond to the problem you want to solve, and let it evolve. Noise and fluctuations can become part of the process—for exploring possibilities or sampling a distribution—rather than something you have to suppress at every step.

That doesn’t mean we need to copy the brain in detail. The inspiration is the organizing principle: computation embodied in the dynamics of a physical system. The challenge is to turn that into something we can engineer, control, and scale.

r001.rationale: It calls the brain an existence proof for useful computation with noisy, dissipative components, but does not communicate that it can perform powerful AI computation.

r002.rationale: It describes electronic circuits using physical dynamics to compute, but does not connect their underlying physics to the brain or say this improves their prospects for brain-like computations.

r003.rationale: It makes no comparison between the mass of electrons and neurotransmitter molecules or their implications for energy efficiency.
